effects.log: The rain drums on the new roof. A young war-god shares her rice with you, and neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Quietly add a small stove to the corner

effects.log: The stove is lit on the first cold day. The war-gods puzzle over who thought of it, and are warm.

events.text: A school for the old custom goes up in {llg_region}, teaching it to anyone who asks. It opens with nine pupils and no speeches. By spring there are forty and a waiting list. The founder's name is not on the lintel, which suits you exactly.

choices.text: Watch the first lesson from the back row

effects.log: The teacher is nervous, the pupils are kind. At the end, a boy of nine bows to the room, and the custom is, once more, alive.

choices.text: Leave your best scroll on the school's shelf

effects.log: The scroll is found and read by an old teacher, who weeps a little and tells no one.

events.text: It took one season to raise, and takes nine to pull down. No one helps at first. Then one morning a boy from the court with the barred doors climbs up and lifts a stone, asking nothing. His father follows. They never speak to you. When the last of the wall is gone the whole court comes to stand in the open air where it used to be.

choices.text: Stand with them and look at the empty place

effects.log: The air is simply air. A woman beside you begins, quietly, to hum. The hum carries across the gap.

choices.text: Slip away before they arrive

effects.log: You leave by the back path. Behind you, you hear the court fill, and the silence that follows is a kind of hymn.

events.text: Bit by bit you take apart what can be taken apart: the custom, the tale, the sealed shrine. It is slow, plain labour and wins you no friends. Then one day a young god asks about the old business and nobody can answer, and a long-held breath goes out of the heavens.

choices.text: Tell the child the plain truth, kindly

effects.log: The child listens, wide-eyed, and nods. It is the first honest account anyone has told in an age.

choices.text: Let the question lapse, as the old business lapses

effects.log: The question drifts off like smoke. Something in the court is lighter for it, and something is lost.

events.text: A priestess named Sobin comes up the temple steps one autumn with a pack and a walking-staff. She tends old shrines, she says, from court to court, because someone ought to and nobody pays. She looks over your work on {llg_thing}, clicks her tongue, and hands you the end of a rope. An hour on, you are halfway up the scaffold.

choices.text: Ask what she counts as an old shrine

effects.log: "Anything older than the roof," she says. "Or kinder." You hold the rope and think about it.

choices.text: Keep holding the rope

effects.log: You hold the rope. The scaffold creaks. Somewhere above, Sobin is humming a hymn you almost know.

events.text: A young god of great wealth arrives to inspect {llg_thing} with a retinue, a poet and a plan to have it gilded. His permits are in order. Sobin plants herself before him with her staff and is gently walked around. He asks you, whom he takes for the foreman, where the gilders should start. A pendant at his throat bears the name of {llg_who}.

choices.text: Point him to the real rot and let his offerings go there

effects.log: He follows your finger, politely baffled. By evening his offerings are in the roof, and Sobin pats your arm.

choices.text: Gently talk him out of the gilding

ok.log: You walk him through the whole place. By the end he is carrying a bucket. Sobin nods approvingly in passing.

fail.log: He will not be moved. The gilders start on the wrong wall, and Sobin sighs for a season.

events.text: A broad godling with a ferryman's hands arrives at your door: Cheon Ma-ra. His shrine has kept an account for five ages, and he wants to read it out to whoever now looks after {llg_thing}, being the nearest thing to the responsible party. He sits and reads for three hours. Names and years, and nothing else. He never lifts his voice.

choices.text: Hear it to the end and ask for a copy

effects.log: He hands you the copy with both hands, as if it were hot. You carry it home and read it again, slowly.

choices.text: Say it was all a very long time ago

effects.log: He stops. The room is cold. He rolls the account and leaves it on the table, which is the cruelest thing he could have done.

events.text: Cheon Ma-ra sends word that his daughter will carry the reckoning from now on. He is tired, he says, and the book is heavy. A small godling with serious eyes appears at the gate with a satchel, and asks if she may read you the first name. She reads it clearly. She has been practising.

choices.text: Listen to all the names, however long it takes

effects.log: The names take the evening. The lamp burns low. When she finishes, she looks at you with grave, tired eyes, and you thank her.

choices.text: Ask her to read slowly, so you can remember them

effects.log: She reads slowly. You say each name after her, softly. By the end you know the first thirty by heart.

events.text: You have grown old tending {llg_thing}. The court has adopted you as a fixture, and the young godlings wave as they pass. At the evening offering an old pilgrim asks whether the place is quiet. "It is," you say, and look at the stair, and for a moment know every foot that ever climbed it. The tea is hot. The air is clean.

choices.text: Sit a while longer

effects.log: You sit. The stair darkens, and the first lamps are lit along it. You are content in a way you have not been for ages.

choices.text: Say good evening to the stair

effects.log: The stair says nothing, as stairs do. But the lamp at its foot flares up, brief and warm.

events.text: You tried to atone, and the ages have worn on, and the work is not finished and never will be. A younger deity has taken up the broom. You tell them what you know. They write it down, and do not ask for more, and that is all you could have asked.

choices.text: Hand over the broom

effects.log: The younger deity takes it in both hands, as if it were a sacred object. You step back, and the sweeping goes on without you.

choices.text: Keep sweeping, since you still can

effects.log: You sweep beside them, stroke for stroke. The dust rises in the late sun, and settles.

events.text: The elders of {ct4_house} have taken a liking to your work, and have drawn up a bond for you in cedar-scented ink: a seat at the lower dais, the hand of {bh4_kin}'s own cousin, and a title in the register. The bond is generous. It is also very long, and on the last page, in smaller script, it says where you may not go.

choices.text: Sign the bond, and take the seat and the cousin

effects.log: The ink dries. The cousin is gracious and well-informed. Your path outward has become a corridor with one door.

choices.text: Return the bond unsigned, with a note of thanks

effects.log: The note is read in silence. {bh4_kin} thanks you in the cold, formal voice of someone who will remember.

events.text: A procession of the elders of {ct4_house} comes to your temple at dawn, in white, with a gift of lacquer boxes. In the boxes are oaths. They are very beautiful oaths. {bh4_kin} reads the first aloud, and the throne it promises, the title {bh4_cap}, is a fine throne. It is also, you notice, the last one they will ever let you sit on.

choices.text: Swear the oaths, and receive the lacquer boxes

effects.log: The oaths are sworn. The boxes are stacked in your hall like a wall, and you feel its shadow in the evenings.

choices.text: Return the boxes, and say you prefer the lower seat that is your own

effects.log: The elders withdraw with perfect courtesy. In the corridor, one of them mutters that you have a poor head for gifts.

events.text: At a feast in the garden of {ct4_house}, you are served the best fish first, and the best wine, and the best seat, and the best hand in marriage. {bh4_kin} raises a cup to your health and your future in the pantheon's service, and every smile at the table is ready, and every smile is the same. You catch a glimpse of the net under the cloth.

choices.text: Raise the cup and accept the pantheon's embrace

effects.log: The cup is cold and sweet. The embrace is warm and absolute. By the end of the season you are the most favoured guest in the house.

choices.text: Set down the cup, and say a guest ought to stay a guest

effects.log: The garden goes quiet. {bh4_kin} lowers the cup carefully, and the smiles slide off the faces like water.

events.text: A messenger arrives with a roll of silk from {ct4_house}, bearing a proposal to adopt you into the lesser branch of the blood. The proposal speaks of your merits in terms so warm they could be hung on a wall. It does not speak of what you would give up. {bh4_kin} waits at the gate with a litter, in case you would like to see your new rooms.

choices.text: Accept the adoption, and climb into the litter

effects.log: The rooms are fine. The window looks onto the courtyard, and the courtyard onto a wall.

choices.text: Send the silk back, folded neatly, with a lamp in the roll

effects.log: The lamp is lit by someone in the house, and put out. {bh4_kin} sends the litter home empty.

events.text: The head-elder of {ct4_house} calls you to the tea room and speaks, pleasantly, about loyalty. The highest throne a guest may reach is {bh4_cap}, and the elder says it with the fondness of a grandmother telling a child where the stairs end. A cup of tea is set before you. The tea is hot, and good, and it holds an oath.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and let the oath settle

effects.log: The oath settles in your chest like a cold coin. The elder smiles, and refills your cup.

choices.text: Leave the tea untouched, and thank the elder for the honour

effects.log: The elder watches you rise, and the pleasant look does not change, which is worse than if it had.

events.text: The lamps in your temple have been put out, one by one, over a month, by an unseen hand. Nobody is caught. Each evening a servant of {ct4_house} calls with a gift basket and an apology. {bh4_kin} will not meet you in the corridor. You have begun to eat in your own rooms, with the door shut and the key in your sleeve.

choices.text: Stay, and keep the lamps lit with your own hands

effects.log: You light them each dusk. Some are put out by morning. You light them again, and the servants learn to avert their eyes.

choices.text: Leave quietly, and take the lamps with you

effects.log: You pack the lamps in straw. The house lets you go without a word, and the corridor behind you is dark.

events.text: Rumours have been planted among the faithful about you: that you skim the tithes, that your altar is cursed, that your hound bit a child. They are told in whispers by the servants of {ct4_house}, who look away when you pass. {bh4_kin} has been seen consoling the child's mother, loudly. The rumour is a good one. It has legs.

choices.text: Stand your ground and answer each rumour before the faithful

effects.log: You answer them, one by one, in the courtyard. Some believe you. The rest watch, and wait, and whisper.

choices.text: Withdraw from the house and its quarrels

effects.log: You withdraw to a smaller shrine, beyond the house's reach. The rumours follow, thinly, and soon lose their legs.

events.text: A summons arrives from the High Table of {ct4_house}: you are charged with having sullied the ancestral tablets. The charge is vague, and the tablets are nowhere named. {bh4_kin}, who delivers it, reads it in a monotone and will not look up. Behind him, the elders sit in a row, like a hedge.

choices.text: Answer the summons, and defend yourself at the High Table

effects.log: You are heard. The hedge does not stir. You leave with the sense that the verdict was written before you arrived, and that you made it a little longer.

choices.text: Ignore the summons, and gather your things

effects.log: You gather them. The hedge does not stir. Your departure is formal, polite and complete.

events.text: The offerings brought to your altar are seized at the gate each dawn by order of {ct4_house}, on the grounds of a technicality no one can quite name. Your worshippers go away in silence. {bh4_kin} sends a letter of regret, in beautiful handwriting. The letter is stamped with a seal that has not been used in a century.

choices.text: Stay, and feed the faithful from your own stores

effects.log: You feed them. The stores shrink. The faithful remember who fed them, and this, in the end, is the house's mistake.

choices.text: Leave the seized altar to the house, and found another elsewhere

effects.log: You found another, on a hill nobody wanted. It is smaller, and it is yours.

events.text: Your hound, the old grey one who has followed you through three domains, comes limping home with its pads cut. Nobody saw anything. A servant of {ct4_house} remarks that these things happen, and that the road to the lower gate is poorly lit. {bh4_kin} offers you a physician, who is very skilled and very quick.

choices.text: Hold your place, and walk the road yourself each night

effects.log: You walk it. The road is dark. Nobody troubles you, and the quiet is an answer.

choices.text: Take the hound and leave the house

effects.log: You carry the hound out in your arms. It licks your chin. The gate swings shut behind you, and does not open again.

events.text: A young scion of {ct4_house} introduces you to a table of her friends as "our famous guest, the one who is not of the blood." They laugh, quietly, behind their sleeves. {bh4_kin}, at the end of the table, is cutting a persimmon with absorbed attention. The persimmon is sweeter than anything said that evening.

choices.text: Laugh along, and ask for a slice of the persimmon

effects.log: The laughter wavers. You eat the slice. It is sweet. The table, uncertain, begins on the next subject.

choices.text: Answer with a courtesy so exact it stings

effects.log: They look up. The scion colours. {bh4_kin} stops cutting and lays the knife down.

events.text: On the day of the clan's ancestral rite, the guests are seated by order of blood, and you are placed at the very end of the last row, below the lamp-trimmers. A card reads: the highest a guest may reach is {bh4_cap}. Someone has propped the card against your cup so that it will not be missed.

choices.text: Sit where you are placed, and eat the rice with good appetite

effects.log: You eat. The rice is warm. By the third course the lamp-trimmers are talking to you, and you find them very good company.

choices.text: Raise the card in a toast, and say nothing

effects.log: The table freezes. You drink. A cousin at the head of the row coughs, and the toast is accepted as a very odd compliment.

events.text: A visiting priest of {ct4_house} says in conversation that your talent is "remarkable for an outsider." He means it generously. He pats your sleeve, and moves on. {bh4_kin}, nearby, nods with all the weight of the pantheon behind the nod. A servant carrying a tray of cups freezes mid-step and then, very carefully, goes on.

choices.text: Take the compliment, and set it aside for later

effects.log: You fold the words away like a letter. They are useful, later, in a quarrel.

choices.text: Ask the priest what the word outsider includes

effects.log: He tries to define it. After the third attempt he gives up, and the servant, passing, brings you a fresh cup.

events.text: A game of questions is played after dinner in the garden of {ct4_house}: each guest must name their ancestors to the ninth degree. You are asked last, and the question hangs. {bh4_kin} stirs the lamp. The scion beside you presses her lips together in what might be pity or might be triumph.

choices.text: Name nine ancestors who were farmers, and mean it

effects.log: You name them, and the garden is quiet. The names are plain, and the quiet is respectful, in the end.

choices.text: Name nine gods who never existed, deadpan

effects.log: The scion chokes on her tea. {bh4_kin} laughs, a short unwilling bark, and the game is abandoned in confusion.

events.text: The elders of {ct4_house} have a saying: the blood rises and the guest sits. Today a child of the blood says it to you, innocently, while stacking cushions. {bh4_kin} is in the next room. The child, noticing your face, tilts her head. "Is it not true?" she asks. "I thought it was nice."

choices.text: Tell her it is true for some, and gently not for others

effects.log: She considers this. "That is more complicated," she says. "I like it better."

choices.text: Help her with the cushions and say nothing

effects.log: You stack them together. When the last is placed, she hands you the topmost one, as a gift.

events.text: Before the whole assembly of {bb_house}, you rise and say it once, without ornament: the {bb_art} is bound to this blood and shall not leave it. The elders nod. The young ones stare. One of the acolytes at the back of the hall, a thin child with ink on her thumbs, whispers the words after you, as if learning a prayer.

choices.text: Hold the child's eye until she lowers hers

effects.log: She lowers it, trembling. The assembly stirs. The binding is spoken, and it holds.

choices.text: Explain, briefly, why you bind it

effects.log: You give your reasons. They are short and honest. The elders listen, and a few of them take notes.

events.text: In the old tongue of the pantheon, you write the binding of the {bb_art} into the family book of {bb_house}, a line at a time, while the eldest daughter holds the lamp. When the last character is dry, she reads it over your shoulder. "It is a heavy line," she says. "I am glad it is yours to write."

choices.text: Close the book and seal it with your thumb

effects.log: The seal is warm. The lamp, held by the eldest daughter, does not waver.

choices.text: Ask her what the book says about the last such binding

effects.log: She turns back a hundred pages. The last binding is there, in a shaking hand, with a single word at the end: regret.

events.text: Envoys from the sister houses of {bb_house} are summoned to the great hall to hear that the {bb_art} is bound to the blood. They sit in their best vestments, hands folded, and the old lord of the neighbouring house is the last to bow. Afterward, in the garden, you can hear them murmuring, and the murmur has a shape.

choices.text: Walk among the envoys and let yourself be seen

effects.log: You walk. They nod, one by one. The old lord does not meet your eye, but he stays until you have passed.

choices.text: Send tea to the garden, and stay in your rooms

effects.log: The tea is drunk and the cups returned. The garden empties slowly, and the murmur goes with it.

events.text: On the feast of open doors, the keepers of {bb_house} recite the house's rules to pilgrims and priests alike, and the {bb_art} is among them. A traveller, footsore from the lower road, asks whether a god's art may be held like a field. A silence falls, and every head turns, and the incense burns on without wind.

choices.text: Answer the traveller yourself, plainly and with respect

effects.log: You answer. The traveller listens, sobered. A few others lean in, and the room warms.

choices.text: Let the high priest answer in the formal cadence

effects.log: The high priest does, in a voice like a bell. The traveller bows. Nobody is quite satisfied, and nobody objects.

events.text: The notice is read aloud at the morning assembly of {bb_house}, between the roster of shrine-duties and a complaint about the offering-store: the {bb_art} is bound to the blood. Anyone who has it keeps it. Anyone who leaves must not use it in sight. The acolyte at your elbow stops chewing. You know the {bb_art}. Everyone knows that you do.

choices.text: Bow with the rest of the assembly

effects.log: You bow. The notice is rolled and filed. The acolyte at your elbow resumes chewing, with great care.

choices.text: Ask aloud what befalls one who forgets

effects.log: The question hangs. The steward clears his throat and says, mildly, that nobody has ever tested it.

events.text: In the guest shrine, a steward-god finds you and reads out, with two heralds standing behind, that the {bb_art} is from today bound to the blood of {bb_house}. You learned it at their table, as a guest. Nobody asks for it back. They want it understood only that you are not kin, and that the roads out of the domain are watched.

choices.text: Thank the steward for coming in person

effects.log: The steward inclines his head. The heralds, behind him, relax their shoulders a hair.

choices.text: Ask who decided it, and when

effects.log: "The elders," says the steward. "Last night." He pauses. "It was a night of two minds."

events.text: A new edict is chalked on the tally-wall of the temple, in the clerk's blocky hand: the {bb_art} is held by the blood of {bb_house} alone. Pilgrims stop to read it on the way to the shrine. Someone has underlined the word alone with a thumbnail, so deeply that the plaster has chipped. You know the {bb_art}, and the clerk knows it.

choices.text: Read the edict aloud to those who cannot read

effects.log: You read it. The pilgrims listen, and some of them bow to you, not knowing why.

choices.text: Brush the dust of the chipped plaster from your sleeve and say nothing

effects.log: You brush the dust. The clerk avoids your eye. The edict stays on the wall until the rain takes it.

events.text: A warden-god of {bb_house} waits on your temple step, with the house's folded tablet in hand and a stillness that is almost a courtesy. {npc} lays the tablet on the stone and turns it so you can read the {bb_art} and your name beneath it. "You were not meant to wield this in the open," {he} says, quite gently. "The house would like it to stop."

choices.text: Agree to put the art away

effects.log: The warden-god nods and takes the tablet. The art is quiet, in your hands, for a season.

choices.text: Tell {him} the house may come and take it

ok.log: {npc} catches your strike, staggers, and sets the tablet down with care. "A fair answer," {he} says, "and a bad bruise."

fail.log: {npc} takes your wrist in a hold that is almost tender and lays you on the flagstones. "I will report that you were asked," {he} says.

choices.text: Offer to pay for what the house taught you

effects.log: The warden-god weighs the offer. "The house will consider," {he} says. The price, when it comes, is fame, and a good deal of it.

events.text: A lacquered case is delivered to your sanctum by {npc}, a quiet warden of {bb_house}, who sets it on the altar and opens it. Within lies a scroll, with the first stanza of the {bb_art} and the seal of the house. "The house asks," {he} says, "what you intend to do with what is written here. There is no hurry. There is no good answer, either."

choices.text: Roll up the scroll and say the art will go quiet

effects.log: {npc} bows and takes the scroll. The art is not used in the open for some time, and the house is satisfied.

choices.text: Hold the scroll out to {him}, and invite {him} to take it

ok.log: {npc} takes the scroll, and with it a fall onto the sanctum floor. "You were always good," {he} says, getting up. "It was never about that."

fail.log: {npc} twists the scroll away and sets you on the floor with a bump. "Please," {he} says, "do not make me ask a third time."

choices.text: Offer the house a season of prayers in its name

effects.log: The offer is accepted, grudgingly, and your fame sinks a little under the weight of an obligation that will not be forgotten.

events.text: Your altar-room door is open, and you did not open it. {npc} sits in the seat that faces the door, drinking your tea, with the air of a person who has long since given up being surprised. "They keep sending me," {he} says. "I would prefer that they stopped. You could arrange it. Or I could. Take your time."

choices.text: Finish your offering, then finish this

ok.log: {npc} rises, courteous, and falls through the doorway in a heap of sleeves. "They told me you would," {he} says, rubbing a shoulder. "I am to say it was well done."

fail.log: {npc} receives your strike in the palm and returns it through the elbow. The altar-room is very quiet while you stand up.

choices.text: Ask for {his} price, and the house's

effects.log: {npc} names it. It is high, and stated without any malice, and your standing in the pantheon pays for it.

events.text: At the gate of your temple at midday, with half the faithful of the district looking on, {npc} unfurls a white banner on a short pole, the old form of reminder. "Third asking," {he} says clearly. "The {bb_art} is the blood's of {bb_house}. You have used it before other pantheons. Let it be settled here, in the open."

choices.text: Take the pole from {him} and accept the reminder

ok.log: You take the pole. {npc} yields at last, and the crowd lets out its breath. The banner comes down, folded in four.

fail.log: {npc} stops the pole with a forearm and takes your guard. The crowd murmurs, and the banner goes up again.

choices.text: Put the art away, aloud, before the faithful

effects.log: You say it. The faithful hush. {npc} lowers the banner and takes your words back to the house.

events.text: The bed has been made with great neatness, and {npc} is not in it. A note on the pillow is in a hand you taught. It does not apologise. It says that the {bb_art} was given freely before it was ever bound, and that {he} wants to see what else the heavens hold. The elders of {bb_house} are in your antechamber. They have not yet knocked.

choices.text: Send your people after {him}

effects.log: Your runners go. The elders watch them leave, and do not say whether they approve.

choices.text: Go after {him} yourself

ok.log: You catch up with {npc} at the second river of light. You talk until the ferry has left twice. {He} comes home, not because you were right but because you came.

fail.log: You find {npc} at the third shrine you try. {He} is doing well. {He} pours you tea, the worst of your existence, and you return alone.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and lift the binding

effects.log: You lift the binding aloud, before the elders. They shift. {npc}, wherever {he} is, is free to use the art as {he} will.

events.text: A ferryman of the upper river mentions it, of all people, while arguing over the price of passage: a young god aboard last month performed an art never seen on these waters, flawlessly, to dry a stranded child's cloak. The ferryman shows you the gesture. It is the {bb_art}. It is {npc}, gone since the thaw, and the elders of {bb_house} knew, and you did not.

choices.text: Send your people after {him}

effects.log: Your people go. The ferryman watches them go, and scratches a chin.

choices.text: Go after {him} yourself

ok.log: You find {npc} asleep on a pile of reeds at a river-shrine. {He} wakes, and the years fall off {him}. You walk back together, and say little.

fail.log: You find {npc} at a river-shrine at dusk, awake and unrepentant. {He} hears you out, pours tea, and goes on watching the water. You walk home alone.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and lift the binding

effects.log: You lift the binding. The ferryman, who has overheard, bows. The art travels on, free.

events.text: Two stewards of the Hall of Names have come a very long way to stand in your court and not quite look at you. The head of the house is tired, they say. Some still speak well of your line. The tablets have been asked, as tablets are asked, and the seal is yours if you will take it: the domains, the feuds, the ledgers, the whole weight of the name. They will wait, but not long.

choices.text: Take the seal

effects.log: The seal is cold and heavier than you thought. The stewards bow, once, and begin at once to speak of the autumn accounts.

choices.text: Not now. Let the head keep the seat

effects.log: The stewards withdraw with perfect courtesy. In the court behind them a single lamp is lit, for the road.

events.text: The herald's letter comes on the house's own gold, sealed in the colour used only for mourning. The head of your blood will step aside if you come. The elders have counted, and you are the one they can bear. You read it three times. It does not say what becomes of what you built here. It does not need to: a house takes all of you.

choices.text: Ascend to the home of your blood, and take the seat

effects.log: You take the road home. The gates are opened by hands that have waited. The seat is cold, and the room is full.

choices.text: Return the letter with a courteous refusal

effects.log: The refusal goes by the morning cloud. The herald reads it, folds it, and carries it away with the air of someone who expected it.
